title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational \(n\times n\) matrix A and every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), outputs a rational Z satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\le Z\le (1+\varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\) in time polynomial in the input bit length and \(1/\varepsilon\)?
definitions: For \(n\ge 1, \operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} A_{i,\pi (i)}\), where \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \([n]\). Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and \(\varepsilon\). There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L},1/\varepsilon )\) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If \(\operatorname{per}(A)=0\), the algorithm must return \(Z=0\) exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of \(\varepsilon\), and the error is relative to \(\operatorname{per}(A)\), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time \(n^{g(1/\varepsilon )}\), does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small \(\varepsilon\) is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

importance.reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda establish an FPRAS for arbitrary nonnegative permanents.
Anari–Rezaei obtain the tight \(2^{n/2}\) guarantee for the Bethe approximation; the result appears at FOCS 2019.
Chen–Vigoda–Yang improve the randomized permanent approximation running time; random sampling remains part of the algorithm.
Anari obtains a deterministic \(c^{n}\) approximation for an absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\); the version checked is revised on 1 September.
Narang–Perkins independently obtain an exponential-base improvement through structural corrections near weighted two-by-two blocks.
Kudria–Luo–Majid give a deterministic polynomial-time \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))\) approximation and explicitly retain the FPTAS question.

context_blocks.text: For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to \(O(n^{6} \log ^{5} n)\) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor \(2^{n/2}\). This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor \(c^{n}\) for some absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\). This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))=\exp (o(n))\). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than \(1+\varepsilon\).

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(A)^{r}\). If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within \(\exp (O(N^{1- \gamma}))\) for one fixed \(\gamma >0\), applying it at \(N=rn\) and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to \(O(n^{1- \gamma}/r^{\gamma})\). Polynomially many copies in n and \(1/\varepsilon\) would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase \(\log (rn)\) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

sentences: The nonnegative permanent sums the weights of all perfect matchings in a bipartite graph.
The question asks for a deterministic approximation within any requested relative error, with fully polynomial running time.
Randomized approximation already achieves this guarantee, so the missing resource is derandomization without sacrificing accuracy.
The saved September review describes deterministic subexponential-factor progress but explains why that factor is still far from one plus epsilon.
Zero entries and arbitrary rational weights are allowed, making bit complexity and reliable handling of very small positive values part of the full target.
